main_damage_causes: Neville's bravery micro-arc — the Leg-Locker Curse incident, Harry's affirmation, and his retaliatory courage in the Quidditch stands — is entirely absent from the film, removing the developmental scaffold that makes his final act of standing up to the trio and Dumbledore's ten-point award emotionally earned rather than abrupt

The film systematically replaces Neville's sympathetic vulnerability with slapstick physical comedy (the flying lesson spectacle), keeping him locked in pure comic-relief register and preventing the audience from investing in him as a character with genuine interior life and growth

Multiple scenes establishing Neville as a persistent, enduring presence in the group's adventures (train compartment, forest detention, midnight wandering) are cut or reduced to offscreen references, thinning his characterisation to isolated pratfall moments rather than a consistent arc across the year

Systematic framing of Neville as pure comic relief – the fainting, the chandelier catchphrase, and the pale-drawing-back beats collectively reduce him to a buffoon identity rather than a sympathetic anxious underdog with genuine arc potential.
Transfer of Snape's public 'matchbox' insult from Neville to Ron removes a defining beat in the Snape/Neville antagonism that is crucial groundwork for Neville's character arc in later books.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Flying lesson: Neville's broom malfunction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 56-57: Neville pushes off early out of nervousness before the whistle, rises uncontrollably, slips sideways off the broom, and falls to the ground breaking his wrist. His broom then drifts away toward the forest. The incident is caused by Neville's fear and jumpiness — a very human, grounded failure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film turns Neville's accident into slapstick spectacle: his broom shoots him uncontrollably around the grounds, he smashes into a wall, clangs along it, zooms past a statue, his cloak catches on a spear, he is flipped off and hangs there, then falls from his cloak onto a torch. The sequence is extended physical comedy with screaming and chaos rather than a brief, pitiful fall.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version emphasises Neville's genuine fear and vulnerability — he is pitiable and sympathetic. The film replaces this with broad cartoon comedy that distances the audience from his emotional reality and frames him purely as comic relief, undermining the quiet pathos the book establishes around his insecurities.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Flying lesson: Neville's Remembrall already in his possession before the fall
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 46-52: Neville receives the Remembrall by owl post at breakfast and Malfoy snatches it at the table; the Remembrall is recovered before the flying lesson begins. During the flying lesson itself, Malfoy picks up the Remembrall from the grass after Neville falls.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses this so that the Remembrall falls from Neville during his flying accident and Malfoy immediately snatches it off the ground, using it as bait to taunt Harry into flying. Neville's quiet moment of showing off his Remembrall at the table, and the separate act of Malfoy stealing it in front of McGonagall (with Neville asserting 'Malfoy's got my Remembrall, Professor'), is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book gives Neville a small but dignified moment — he proudly explains the Remembrall, and then calls out Malfoy directly to McGonagall. The film removes this moment of mild assertiveness and reduces Neville to a passive prop whose object is simply taken and used to motivate Harry.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Train: Neville absent from compartment scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 4-16: Neville appears in person on the train, knocking on Harry and Ron's compartment twice while searching for Trevor, and is taken away by Hermione at the end. He is a physically present, tearful, sympathetic character introduced organically alongside Harry's first friendships.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neville is entirely absent from the train compartment. His existence is only referenced by Hermione's line 'Has anyone seen a toad? A boy named Neville's lost one.' Neville himself never appears or speaks on the train.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the train to establish Neville as a recurring, endearing presence — lost, anxious, but persistent. His repeated visits to the compartment humanise him. The film reduces him to a name mentioned offscreen, losing his first introduction as a sympathetic character and delaying the audience's relationship with him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Sorting: Neville's toad moment at the castle entrance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 30: During the Sorting, Neville falls over on his way to the stool, the hat takes a long time to decide, and he runs off still wearing it, returning amid laughter. The book also notes McGonagall's eye lingering on Neville's cloak fastened under his left ear before the ceremony.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neville's only moment at the castle entrance/sorting is catching Trevor near McGonagall's feet, looking embarrassed, and backing away while students laugh. His actual Sorting is not depicted — it is skipped entirely. None of his stumbling to the stool or the hat's deliberation is shown.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Sorting moment reinforces Neville's clumsiness but also the hat's genuine deliberation over him — a small seed of his hidden depth. The film skips his Sorting entirely, losing this beat and replacing it with pure physical comedy (chasing the toad), keeping him squarely in the buffoon register.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 — Halloween: Neville reports Hermione crying in the bathroom
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not feature Neville delivering this information; Harry and Ron learn about Hermione being upset through other means. In the book, Neville is not a conduit for social information between the main trio.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neville delivers the line: 'Parvati Patil said that she wouldn't come out of the girls' bathroom. She said she'd been in there all afternoon, crying.' This is Neville's only dialogue in the Halloween sequence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a minor addition rather than a damaging removal, but it reduces Neville to a functional information-delivery role with no characterisation of his own. His presence in the scene is purely instrumental rather than revealing anything about him. Low damage but keeps him in the peripheral, functional register.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 — Common room: Neville confronts the trio before the trapdoor
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 169-185: Neville blocks the portrait hole, raises his fists ('Go on then, try and hit me! I'm ready!'), and delivers the defiant line 'Don't you call me an idiot! I don't think you should be breaking any more rules! And you were the one who told me to stand up to people!' He is then hit with Petrificus Totalus and left on the floor. The book frames this as a moment of real courage — 'it takes a great deal of bravery to stand up to our friends.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes this scene and Neville does say 'I won't let you! You'll get Gryffindor into trouble again! I-I'll fight you.' and holds out his fists, and is Petrified. However, Neville's most pointed line — invoking Ron's own advice to stand up to people — is absent. The emotional resonance of Neville demonstrating he has internalised the lesson is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film captures the physical beat but loses the thematic heart of the moment: Neville quoting Ron's own words back at him ('You were the one who told me to stand up to people!') is what makes his defiance intellectually coherent and emotionally earned rather than just reactive. Without it, the scene is brave but less pointed, and its connection to Dumbledore's later award of ten points for standing up to friends is weakened.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 — End-of-year feast: Neville's ten points
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 187: Dumbledore says 'It takes a great deal of bravery to stand up to our enemies, but just as much to stand up to our friends. I therefore award ten points to Mr. Neville Longbottom.' Neville goes white with shock and disappears under a pile of people hugging him. The book notes he had never won so much as a point for Gryffindor before.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dumbledore says 'it takes a great deal of bravery to stand up to your enemies, but a great deal more to stand up to your friends. I award 10 points to Neville Longbottom.' Neville reacts with disbelief. The scene is present and largely faithful in content.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film preserves this scene well. The only minor damage is that the prior context — Neville's confrontation in the common room — was slightly stripped of its thematic sharpness, so the payoff here, while present, lands with somewhat less earned weight. The scene itself is not unfaithful; the damage is upstream.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Potions class: Neville's cauldron incident absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 39-42: Neville melts Seamus's cauldron, their potion seeps across the floor burning holes in shoes, and Neville is drenched in boiling potion with angry red boils springing up all over his arms, legs, and nose. Snape snarls 'Idiot boy!' and then uses the incident to unfairly attack Harry. Neville is taken to the hospital wing by Seamus.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Potions class scene in the film focuses entirely on Snape interrogating Harry. Neville's cauldron explosion — his most prominent academic failure, establishing both his Potions weakness and Snape's cruelty toward him — does not appear in the film corpus at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is important for Neville on multiple levels: it shows his academic vulnerability in Potions (his worst subject), it shows him suffering genuine physical harm, and it contextualises why he fears Snape. Its absence removes a key piece of his characterisation and also removes a scene where Snape's bullying of students through Neville is made concrete. His later exam note about scraping through with his Herbology mark compensating for abysmal Potions has no grounding in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — Absent: Quidditch match courage scenes (Leg-Locker Curse and stands fight)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 110-131: Neville arrives in the common room with the Leg-Locker Curse on him, having been attacked by Malfoy outside the library. He refuses to report it ('I don't want more trouble'). Harry gives him his last Chocolate Frog and says 'You're worth twelve of Malfoy.' Neville then stands up to Malfoy in the Quidditch stands ('I'm worth twelve of you, Malfoy'), and during the match physically fights Crabbe and Goyle, ending up unconscious but having stood his ground.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: None of these scenes appear in the film corpus. The Leg-Locker Curse incident, Harry's 'you're worth twelve of Malfoy' moment, Neville's echo of those words in the stands, and Neville fighting Crabbe and Goyle are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most significant arc damage in the corpus. These scenes collectively form Neville's central developmental beat in Book 1: he is victimised, shown genuine compassion by Harry, internalises a message of self-worth, and then acts on it in the stands. This is the direct precursor to his confrontation in the common room and Dumbledore's award of points. Without it, Neville's bravery arc has no middle act — the audience sees him as fearful and clumsy, then suddenly defiant in the common room, without the intermediate steps that make his growth believable and moving. Harry's relationship with Neville as someone who actively champions him is also lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — Absent: Forest detention sequence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 147-162: Neville has a detention in the Forbidden Forest alongside Harry, Hermione, and Malfoy. He is frightened but present, clutches Harry's robe, and is paired with Malfoy and Fang in a separate group. Malfoy sneaks up on Neville as a joke and Neville panics and sends up red sparks. Harry internally reflects 'if something's got Neville... it's our fault he's here in the first place.' Neville is shown as frightened but enduring a genuine ordeal.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The forest detention sequence does not appear in the film corpus at all. Neville is entirely absent from this section.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The detention scene gives Neville one of his more sustained presences in the story and reinforces his vulnerability alongside genuine loyalty — he endures the forest even though he is terrified. Harry's guilt about Neville being there because of them adds relational depth. Its absence removes another instance of Neville being tested and enduring, contributing to the thinning of his arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — Absent: Night-time wandering / trophy room chase
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 70-95: Neville is found curled asleep outside the common room having forgotten the password, joins the group for the midnight duel, trips and grabs Ron into a suit of armor causing a loud crash, and after reaching the forbidden corridor is described as looking as if he'd never speak again. He is shown as someone who gets caught up in events and causes problems through panic, but also someone who sticks with the group.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire sequence — Neville found outside, joining the midnight outing, causing the armor crash, witnessing Fluffy — is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This sequence establishes Neville as a recurring presence in the trio's misadventures and shows his comic-but-genuine panic causing real consequences. It also gives him a shared experience of the Fluffy corridor, which contextualises his later horror about it. Its absence further reduces his screen presence and removes group dynamic material.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Cornish Pixie lesson: Neville draws back pale before the cage is opened
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 25 establishes Neville 'cowering in his front row seat' before the cage opens – consistent with his anxious nature, but this is one beat among many where the class collectively reacts.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The screenplay singles out Neville with a dedicated beat: 'A pale Neville draws back' while Harry and Ron lean forward, framing Neville as the sole fearful contrast to the protagonists' curiosity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor reinforcement of Neville-as-coward framing. The book also has him cowering so this is not a full departure, but the film sharpens the contrast by juxtaposing his pallor directly against Harry and Ron's eagerness, slightly exaggerating his fearfulness as a visual gag setup.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Cornish Pixie lesson: Neville lifted and dropped from the chandelier
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 28 and 31 show pixies seizing Neville by the ears, lifting him to the chandelier, and him falling when it gives way – this is present in both book and film and is played for chaos comedy in both.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the physical beat but adds Neville's line 'Why is it always me?' after he plops onto Lockhart's desk – a self-aware comedic line not present in the book corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The added line 'Why is it always me?' reframes Neville's humiliation as self-aware comic relief and a recurring catchphrase, reducing it to a punchline identity. The book Neville endures mishaps without this resigned, self-deprecating awareness; he is anxious and accident-prone but not a character who narrates his own misfortune as a joke. This small addition incrementally builds Neville as the series' comic butt rather than a sympathetic underdog.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Greenhouse Three) – Neville faints at the Mandrake
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not contain a Mandrake-repotting scene for CoS. There is no book evidence in the provided corpus of Neville fainting at a Mandrake. The book establishes Neville as accident-prone and anxious (Book Scene 8) but the corpus does not include this specific scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1 (Greenhouse Three, Scene 40) shows Neville's 'eyes ROLL BACK. He FAINTS' at the sight of the Mandrake baby, and is left lying on the ground while the class continues. Sprout initially misattributes it to him neglecting his earmuffs, and the class simply moves on around his prone body.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene plays Neville's anxiety as pure physical comedy – he faints so completely he is left on the greenhouse floor like discarded equipment. While his nervousness is book-accurate in general, the faint-and-be-ignored treatment reduces him to a prop for a visual gag. The corpus does not provide a book counterpart to this specific scene, so the damage is assessed at medium confidence, but the framing is clearly an escalation of his buffoonery beyond what the book corpus supports.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Dueling Club) – Snape's dismissal of Neville replaced by dismissal of Ron's wand
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 52 establishes a specific, named humiliation of Neville: Snape says 'Longbottom causes devastation with the simplest spells. We'll be sending what's left of Finch-Fletchley up to the hospital wing in a matchbox.' This is directed at Neville personally and publicly, in front of the whole club.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 2 (Dueling Club, Scene 70) transfers the insult to Ron: 'Weasley's wand causes devastation with the simplest spells. We'll be sending Potter to the hospital wing in a matchbox.' Neville is not singled out at all in this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a meaningful transfer of a defining Neville moment. In the book, Snape's public dismissal of Neville in front of the entire school is part of the established pattern of Neville being belittled by Snape – a relationship dynamic that underpins Neville's arc (his greatest fear in PoA is Snape, not Voldemort). By redirecting the insult to Ron, the film loses a key data point in Snape's specific cruelty toward Neville and removes Neville's public humiliation before peers. The insult still lands in the narrative but now belongs to the Harry/Ron/Snape dynamic rather than developing Neville's situation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Hospital Wing visit) – Neville's tubeworm loan as social barometer
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not directly contain this exchange, but the film (Scene 90) has Harry tell Hermione: 'Neville asked to borrow a tubeworm in Potions yesterday. I suppose that's something.' This is used to indicate Harry's social isolation – Neville is the one person still willing to speak to him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 (Scene 90): Harry uses Neville's minimal contact as the sole sign that anyone is still treating him normally, framing Neville as socially peripheral – someone whose acknowledgement barely counts as social acceptance.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a minor but telling framing issue. Neville is presented as the lowest rung of social acceptance – the one person pathetic enough to still speak to Harry when everyone else has turned away. While this may be tonally consistent with CoS's social-isolation arc for Harry, it reinforces Neville's positioning as an outcast even among Gryffindors, which subtly damages his standing without book corpus evidence to support this specific framing.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Gryffindor Common Room after Hermione's Petrification) – Neville's speech about Slytherins
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 40 establishes Neville buying protective talismans out of fear, and Book Scene 41 shows him saying 'They went for Filch first, and everyone knows I'm almost a Squib' – Neville's fear is personal, inward, and rooted in his own self-doubt about his magical ability.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 (Scene 108): Neville delivers a notably assertive speech – 'Haven't any of the teachers noticed that the Slytherins are all safe? Isn't it obvious all this stuff's coming from Slytherin? The Heir of Slytherin, the monster of Slytherin – why don't they just chuck all the Slytherins out?' This is a confident, outward-directed political observation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a curious reversal of the book's Neville. The corpus shows Neville as self-doubting and fearful (buying talismans, worrying about being a Squib, timid reactions). The film gives him a moment of surprisingly bold, almost aggressive political clarity that is inconsistent with his established characterization in this corpus. While not gravely damaging, it represents a tonal inconsistency – the film occasionally grants Neville confident quips (also 'Why is it always me?') that collectively shift him from anxious underdog toward comic-relief pundit, which is a different character register.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 (Flying Car) – Neville and Seamus visible in train window
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 65 places Neville asleep in the dormitory while Harry and Ron discuss their plans; Book Scene 8 establishes he greeted them 'cheerfully' on arrival. There is no book corpus evidence of Neville observing the flying car from the train.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1 (Scene 34): As the car nearly collides with the Hogwarts Express, Harry 'glimpses NEVILLE and SEAMUS, mouths open in astonishment' in a train window.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor addition with negligible damage. Neville is used as a background reaction shot to sell the comedy of the near-collision. No characterization damage, but it is an invention not grounded in the book corpus.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Boggart lesson: Lupin whispers instructions to Neville privately
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lupin publicly walks Neville through the entire plan — asking him about his grandmother's clothes, describing exactly what will happen, building Neville's confidence visibly in front of the class. The preparation is transparent and communal, emphasising Lupin's gift for drawing out students.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lupin leans in and whispers the instructions to Neville privately ('We don't need to hear it. If you see it, we will.'). The audience and class are excluded from the preparation. Neville's moment of being coached and trusted is rendered opaque.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's public coaching scene shows Lupin's teaching philosophy and his deliberate investment in Neville specifically. The film's whisper removes the warmth of that exchange, though Neville still succeeds, so the damage is minor.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Boggart lesson: Neville does not finish the boggart off with a second charge
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Neville a two-beat triumph: after the first Riddikulus the boggart becomes a cockroach and snaps back to Snape, so Neville charges forward a second time looking determined, laughs, and the boggart explodes. Lupin awards him ten points for doing it twice. Neville's arc in the scene is one of escalating courage.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Neville cast Riddikulus once, the class laughs, and Lupin immediately moves on to Ron. The second charge and the boggart's destruction by Neville's laughter are absent. Lupin does not award specific points to Neville.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Neville's double victory — and the explicit reward of ten points — is one of his clearest early agency moments in the series. Reducing it to a single beat diminishes the arc of courage the scene is designed to give him and removes Lupin's public, named commendation of him.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Potions class / Snape bullying: entirely absent from film corpus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Potions as Neville's worst subject and the site of his most sustained humiliation. Snape publicly threatens to poison Trevor if Neville's potion fails, Neville is 'breathless with fear' and begs Hermione for help, Crabbe and Goyle laugh openly, and the entire class watches Neville sweat. Despite this, the potion works — a small, hard-won success.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No Potions scene featuring Neville's fear, Snape's bullying of him, or Trevor's near-poisoning appears in the film corpus. This extended characterisation is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Potions scenes are the primary site where the books establish the depth of Neville's fear under Snape, his resilience, and the specific texture of his suffering. Without them, the boggart scene (Snape as worst fear) loses its grounding — film audiences are not shown why Snape is so terrifying to Neville specifically, weakening the emotional logic of the boggart sequence and Neville's characterisation as someone who endures systematic cruelty.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Snape's classroom doorway insult to Lupin about Neville: absent from film corpus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Snape pauses at the doorway before the boggart lesson and tells Lupin not to trust Neville with anything difficult, publicly humiliating him in front of another teacher. Lupin's deliberate, warm counter — 'I was hoping Neville would assist me' — is a direct rebuttal that makes Neville go even redder but also demonstrates an adult publicly championing him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This exchange does not appear in the film corpus. Snape is present (he mutters 'It's this class that's ridiculous') but the targeted public humiliation of Neville at the doorway and Lupin's specific public defence of him are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Snape–Lupin doorway exchange is the clearest moment in the book where an adult openly champions Neville against systematic cruelty. Its absence removes a key beat in the Lupin–Neville relationship and weakens the sense that Lupin sees and values Neville in ways others do not.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Gryffindor pyjama gathering / Neville confesses to losing passwords [CUT SCENE]
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Neville a full, specific accountability beat: trembling in his fluffy slippers, he slowly raises his hand before the entire house and McGonagall. He is punished concretely (banned from Hogsmeade, forced to wait outside the tower nightly, receives a Howler). This sequence is important to Neville's characterisation as someone who makes serious mistakes but faces consequences with a kind of helpless honesty.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is listed as a cut non-theatrical scene and must be treated as absent from the film. The confession, the punishments, and the Howler are all lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's password subplot gives Neville a consequential mistake with real social and disciplinary fallout, followed by public shame (the Howler). The film corpus retains only the Sir Cadogan scene where Neville mentions keeping a list, and the film's pyjama confession scene is cut. Without the accountability arc, Neville's role in Black's break-in collapses to a background detail rather than a thread of his own characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Sir Cadogan / password scene: Neville keeping a list treated as comedy only
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Neville's password difficulties as a genuine recurring vulnerability rooted in his poor memory and anxiety, not merely comic incompetence. The list is a coping strategy born of real distress ('I must've dropped them somewhere!'), and he pleads tearfully with Sir Cadogan.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film corpus (Scene 11), Neville holds up the list and notes Sir Cadogan keeps changing the password twice in one morning, framed as a mildly comic aside. There is no tearfulness, no pleading, and no visible distress — it reads as an exasperated practical response.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but consistent: the film flattens Neville's anxious vulnerability into mild comic exasperation, losing the specific emotional texture the book gives to even his small failures.

damaging_scenes.scene: PoA Film - Divination class: Neville's broken cups and Trelawney's ominous predictions reduced
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Neville two broken cups, Trelawney's dramatic swoon, her cryptic 'my poor dear boy... no, it is kinder not to say,' her prediction he will be late, and the class lingering on 'but what about Neville's cup?' as a serious omen. Neville is marked out as someone shadowed by dark prophecy.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus (Scene 6) shows Trelawney predict the cup breaking before it happens ('after you've broken your first cup...') and Neville duly drops it. The ominous follow-up — the swoon, the cryptic refusal to say what she sees, the class's unease about his cup — is absent. It plays as a single comic beat.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Trelawney's treatment of Neville to seed his association with ill omen and inherited darkness (later relevant to his family history). The film reduces this to a single physical gag, losing the atmospheric weight around Neville specifically.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Defense Against the Dark Arts, Unforgivable Curses lesson
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes that Neville raises his hand to answer Moody's question about illegal curses – an act of unusual daring that surprises even Neville himself ('Neville looked surprised at his own daring'). He answers 'in a small but distinct voice.' His reaction to the Cruciatus demonstration is one of silent, clenched, white-knuckled horror – a deeply private trauma response rooted in his parents' fate, which the reader senses but does not yet understand.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Neville is called upon or walks to the front of the classroom rather than volunteering. The film shows him visibly frightened by the spider demonstration itself, with his fear played for a degree of comic effect as the spider is directed at him first to get a laugh from the class. The internal, dignified horror of his book reaction is flattened into more generic timidity and fright.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Neville shows a rare moment of courage by volunteering, then endures the Cruciatus demonstration with a restrained, deeply personal anguish. The film replaces the volunteering with apparent compulsion and uses Neville as comic relief with the spider, stripping the dignity from what is actually a profoundly traumatic moment for him. The quiet courage of raising his hand – unusual enough to surprise himself – is lost entirely.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Hallway after the Unforgivable Curses lesson
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: After the lesson, the book shows Neville standing alone in a side passage, staring at the wall with wide, horrified eyes. When approached, he speaks in a much higher-than-usual voice, gabbling incoherently about dinner and food – a vivid portrayal of dissociation and suppressed trauma. He looks 'pleadingly' at Harry, Ron, and Hermione when Moody steers him away. Later, in the dormitory, his eyes are red, implying he has been crying. The book explicitly notes Harry realizes Neville was lying awake that night, not sleeping, revealing the depth of his distress.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows 'Moody' walking up to Neville after the lesson and Neville nodding, then the two walk back to the classroom together. The entire extended hallway scene – Neville's dissociative gabbling, Hermione's gentle concern, the pleading look, the red eyes in the dormitory, the sleepless night – is absent. Neville's trauma is not dramatized beyond the classroom.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The hallway and dormitory aftermath is the moment that humanizes Neville most deeply in Goblet of Fire and plants the emotional seed for the revelation about his parents. Losing it removes the audience's ability to feel the weight of Neville's private suffering before that revelation arrives. It also cuts Hermione's empathetic response to Neville, which is a small but meaningful relationship beat.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Moody lending Neville 'Magical Water Plants of the Mediterranean'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes that after taking Neville for tea, Moody lends him the book 'Magical Water Plants of the Mediterranean' and tells Neville that Professor Sprout said he was really good at Herbology. The narrator notes: 'Telling Neville what Professor Sprout had said, Harry thought, had been a very tactful way of cheering Neville up, for Neville very rarely heard that he was good at anything.' Neville relays this 'with a faint note of pride' – a rare emotional uplift. The book also later reveals this was a deliberate plant by the disguised Barty Crouch Jr. to get gillyweed information to Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 3, Neville mentions the book ('Moody gave it to me. That day we had tea'), but the detail about Professor Sprout's praise – and the emotional weight of Neville rarely hearing he is good at anything – is absent. The book is referenced only instrumentally, as a lead-in to the gillyweed solution.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's handling of Moody's gift is a rare moment of Neville receiving affirmation and feeling pride. Stripping the Sprout praise reduces a small but genuine character beat to a plot convenience, slightly diminishing the texture of Neville's low self-esteem and the significance of rare encouragement to him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Second Task: Neville gives Harry the gillyweed
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes that the gillyweed solution was engineered entirely by the disguised Moody/Barty Crouch Jr., who planted the book with Neville and expected Harry to ask Neville for help. Harry never does – Dobby ultimately obtains the gillyweed from Snape's stores on Neville's behalf after reading the book. Neville's role is passive and indirect; the agency rests with Dobby and Moody's manipulation. Neville is a conduit, not an active helper.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 7, Neville directly gives Harry the gillyweed and is the active, decisive helper. He tells Harry to use gillyweed, Harry asks him if he's sure, and Neville confirms it (with some comic hedging about fresh vs. salt water). Neville then watches anxiously and panics when Harry seems to be choking, crying 'Oh, my God. I've killed Harry Potter.' This makes Neville a meaningful, proactive agent in Harry's survival.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is actually a transfer of agency that upgrades Neville's role rather than damaging it in the traditional sense – Neville becomes more heroic and useful. However, it does misrepresent the book's characterization: book-Neville is not yet the person who confidently steps up to help Harry in a crisis; that arc is in the future. The film grants him competence and agency he has not yet earned in the narrative, which is a faithful portrayal issue even if superficially flattering. It also removes the thematic point that Harry failed to utilize the people around him (including Neville) – a moral Moody/Crouch intended to teach. The film's Neville proactively offering help erases that missed opportunity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 / Scene 6 – Yule Ball: Neville dancing with Ginny
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes that Neville asked Hermione to the ball (she was 'already going with someone') and then asked Ginny after Hermione turned him down. Ginny accepts, looking 'extremely miserable.' At the ball, Neville is seen treading on Ginny's feet while dancing – a small, comic but humanizing detail. The book also establishes the backstory of Neville asking Hermione via Ron's retelling, which reveals Neville recognizes Hermione's kindness to him ('She's always been really nice, helping him out with work and stuff').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Neville dancing with Ginny at the ball (Film Scene 5/6) – this beat is present. However, the entire preceding arc of Neville asking Hermione and being turned down (Ron's account of it, including his dismissive 'I mean, who would?') is absent from the film corpus. The Yule Ball dancing appearance is brief and backgrounded.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's account of Neville asking Hermione reveals something important: Neville recognizes genuine kindness when he receives it and is capable of social initiative, however awkward. Ron's cruel dismissal ('who would go with Neville?') also contextualizes how Neville is perceived by peers. Losing this exchange removes a meaningful beat about Neville's social position, his appreciation of Hermione, and his quiet courage in attempting to find a date. The film reduces him to a background dancing figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 9 (Pensieve sequence) – Trial of Barty Crouch Jr. and the Longbottoms
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes a rich emotional aftermath to Harry witnessing the Pensieve trial: Dumbledore explains that Frank and Alice Longbottom were tortured into insanity, are in St. Mungo's, and do not recognize Neville. Harry is 'horror-struck' and reflects on four years of knowing Neville without ever asking about his parents. Dumbledore asks Harry not to tell anyone – 'He has the right to let people know, when he is ready.' Harry lies awake that night thinking about Neville's situation, feeling Neville 'deserved' sympathy more than Harry did as an orphan. The trial scene in the Pensieve also names Frank Longbottom explicitly as the tortured Auror.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Pensieve sequence includes the trial of Barty Crouch Jr. and the naming of Frank Longbottom as the tortured Auror (Film Scene 9: 'I know for a fact this person took part in the capture, and, by means of the Cruciatus Curse, torture of the Auror Frank Longbottom and his wife!'). However, the subsequent conversation between Harry and Dumbledore about Neville – the revelation of his parents' fate, Harry's guilt at never asking, Dumbledore's instruction to keep the secret, and Harry's reflective sympathy – is entirely absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Pensieve trial names Neville's parents, but without the Dumbledore conversation that follows, the connection to Neville is never made explicit for the audience. The film viewer who does not know the books has no reliable way to connect Frank Longbottom to Neville. This cuts the most significant Neville material in the entire book – the revelation of his parents' fate, Harry's empathetic reckoning, and the establishment of Neville as a character with a tragic backstory that rivals Harry's own. It severs a key piece of Neville's arc and removes the moral complexity Dumbledore adds about Neville's right to share his own story. This is the single most damaging absence in the corpus.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Imperious Curse classroom demonstration
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book shows Neville performing 'a series of quite astonishing gymnastics he would certainly not have been capable of in his normal state' under the Imperius Curse, and 'not one of them seemed to be able to fight off the curse.' This is a small but telling detail: even under Imperius, Neville is described with a kind of inadvertent physical comedy, but also the serious point that he cannot resist the curse.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's DADA classroom scene (Film Scene 1) shows Moody directing the spider at Neville and others but does not appear to depict the Imperius Curse demonstration being performed on Neville individually. The gymnastics beat is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor loss – the gymnastics detail is lightly comic but also establishes Neville's inability to resist the Imperius Curse, which has thematic resonance. Its absence is a small texture loss rather than a structural one.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Train journey to Hogwarts (carriage scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Neville is actively characterised on the train: he proudly shows off his Mimbulus mimbletonia, explains its properties with genuine enthusiasm, demonstrates it (causing the Stinksap explosion), introduces himself to Luna, and asserts 'I'm nobody' when Luna stares at him - showing his self-deprecating insecurity but also his warmth and his passion for Herbology. He is also the one who introduces the password 'Mimbulus mimbletonia' to the Fat Lady, showing he remembered it because the plant matters to him.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses the entire train journey. Neville appears briefly to say 'Hi, guys' and nothing more. The Mimbulus mimbletonia, the Stinksap incident, the awkward Luna introduction, and Neville's self-deprecating 'I'm nobody' line are all absent. His defining passion for Herbology and his characteristic mix of clumsiness and enthusiasm are entirely lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The train scene is the book's primary early establishment of Neville's independent personality in OotP - his specialist passion, his social awkwardness, his warmth. Losing it means the film Neville arrives at Hogwarts as a near-blank, with no distinctive trait introduced.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Neville defends Harry to Seamus in the dormitory
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Seamus challenges Harry and Ron demands to know who else doubts Harry, Neville speaks up clearly and simply: 'My gran says that's rubbish... We believe Harry. My gran's always said You-Know-Who would come back one day. She says if Dumbledore says he's back, he's back.' He then climbs into bed and gazes fondly at his moonlit cactus. This is a moment of quiet moral courage and loyalty, and it establishes Neville as someone who stands by Harry independently, not just as a sidekick.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is listed in the non-theatrical exclusions ('Neville defends Harry' cut scene) and does not appear in the theatrical film. Neville's early act of loyalty and moral backbone is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of Neville's most quietly courageous moments in the early book - he speaks up unprompted when others are silent or hostile. Its absence removes evidence of Neville's independent moral courage and his personal connection to believing in Voldemort's return (given his family's history). The film loses a beat that would later make his DoM arc more resonant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Neville with Mimbulus mimbletonia in the dormitory / 'Life in Gryffindor Tower'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Neville tenderly placing his Mimbulus mimbletonia on his bedside cabinet, gazing fondly at his moonlit cactus, and later asking about Seamus's summer - all small beats that build a portrait of Neville as caring, gentle, and defined by his Herbology passion even in private moments.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This material falls under the cut 'Life in Gryffindor Tower' scene, which is excluded from the theatrical film. The Mimbulus mimbletonia never appears on screen at all in a meaningful character-building context.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The plant is a recurring symbol of Neville's character in OotP - his passion, his pride, and even his memory (the password). Its complete absence from the film strips away the single most concrete personality marker the book gives him in this instalment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - DA meeting, Neville's first Expelliarmus
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Neville is left partnerless (characteristically), Harry partners him, Neville's wand goes flying off a bookshelf and Harry retrieves it with a Summoning Charm. Then Neville catches Harry off-guard and succeeds: 'I DID IT! I've never done it before - I DID IT!' His joy is genuine and hard-won, and Harry notes privately that in a real duel Neville's opponent wouldn't be looking away - keeping Neville's limitations realistic even in his triumph.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Neville performing Expelliarmus in the DA session, and Harry says 'Fantastic, Neville. Well done, man.' However, the film presents this within a montage of general DA activity. The specific narrative of Neville being left partnerless, Harry choosing to work with him, the wand flying off the shelf, and most importantly Neville's ecstatic 'I DID IT! I've never done it before!' is not rendered with the same emotional weight. The scene exists but is compressed into a general training sequence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book beat is present in attenuated form - the film does show Neville succeeding at Expelliarmus and Harry praising him. The specific emotional texture of Neville's breakthrough (the first-time success, his exultation, the realistic caveat Harry keeps private) is flattened into a training montage, mildly reducing its impact but not eliminating the beat entirely.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Neville's reaction to Death Eaters' escape (newspaper scene / DA intensification)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book devotes explicit attention to the effect of Bellatrix Lestrange's escape on Neville. He undergoes 'a strange and even slightly alarming change': he stops talking during DA meetings but works 'relentlessly on every new jinx and counter-curse', 'apparently indifferent to injuries or accidents', and only Hermione masters the Shield Charm faster than him. This is one of the most important characterisation moments in OotP - Neville's silent, focused rage becoming the engine of his growth.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Neville reading the newspaper about the escape (he is shown holding it as Bellatrix's escape is revealed). However, the subsequent 'alarming change' - the silent intensity, the relentless training, the explicit narrative of his accelerated improvement as a response to his parents' torturer being free - is not depicted. The film does not trace this arc of transformation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the book's central arc beat for Neville in OotP: his personal motivation for fighting, expressed not in words but in silent, focused effort. The film shows him reacting to the news but does not dramatise the transformation. Without it, Neville's DoM bravery appears as generic group loyalty rather than deeply personal vengeance and courage rooted in his parents' suffering. This materially damages the emotional coherence of his arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - St Mungo's Hospital ward visit
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's St Mungo's scene is one of the most affecting in the entire series for Neville. It establishes: his mortified shame at being discovered, his grandmother's blunt pride ('they didn't give their health and their sanity so their only son would be ashamed of them'), his quiet 'I'm not ashamed' (said faintly, not convincingly), his mother giving him a Drooble's wrapper, his quiet 'Thanks, Mum', his defiant expression daring others to laugh, and - crucially - Harry watching him slip the wrapper into his pocket. The scene also establishes that Neville has never told his friends about his parents.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The St Mungo's scene does not appear anywhere in the film corpus. It is entirely absent from the theatrical film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is arguably the single most damaging omission for Neville's arc. The St Mungo's scene is the emotional foundation for everything Neville does at the DoM: his determination to avenge his parents, his quiet dignity, his complicated feelings of shame and love, his relationship with his grandmother. Without it, the DoM confrontation with Bellatrix ('Better, now they're about to be avenged') loses its full emotional grounding. The audience does not witness the scene that explains why Neville fights so hard - they are told about his parents' fate only in passing (via Sirius in Film Scene 1) without the direct, devastating personal encounter.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Malfoy mocking Neville's parents / Neville charging at Malfoy
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Malfoy makes a grotesque face mocking someone (implied to be connected to Neville's parents), Neville 'collided hard with Harry's shoulder, heading straight for Malfoy' in a sudden explosion of rage. Harry has to physically restrain him, Ron seizes his arms, and Neville's choked words ('Not...funny...don't...Mungo's...show...him') hint at his parents without revealing them. After being dragged back, Neville snatches his bag and stalks off, still furious. This establishes that beneath Neville's gentle exterior is genuine fierce protectiveness about his parents.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus. There is no equivalent moment where Neville physically lunges at Malfoy in defence of his parents' honour.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Malfoy confrontation is one of two moments (the other being St Mungo's) that reveal Neville's fierce, barely-contained anger about his parents. Without it, the film Neville has no visible emotional response to his parents' situation before the DoM, making his DoM behaviour harder to read as personal rather than simply brave. The scene also shows Neville exercising a kind of agency - acting impulsively on a deep emotion - that the film's Neville never demonstrates.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Neville's Patronus difficulty / Patronus training scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, during Patronus training, Neville has serious trouble: 'only feeble wisps of silver smoke issued from his wand tip'. Harry reminds him to think of something happy; Neville is 'trying so hard his round face was actually shining with sweat', saying 'I'm trying' miserably. This is a specific, named moment of Neville struggling with the happiest-memory requirement - plausibly because his happiest memories are complicated by his family situation.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Patronus training sequence is a general montage. Neville is shown successfully casting Expelliarmus during this sequence, but the specific scene of him struggling with the Patronus Charm while sweating with effort is not present as a distinct beat in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor but telling omission: the book uses Neville's Patronus difficulty as a subtle, unspoken suggestion that his emotional landscape is darker than his cheerful exterior suggests. The film's montage format loses this nuance, though the impact is limited.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - DoM battle: Neville's broken nose and refusal to give up ('Whaddever you do, Harry, don'd gib it to him!')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after Dolohov breaks Neville's wand and kicks him in the face (breaking his nose), Neville - bleeding heavily, face swollen - still tells Harry fiercely not to give the prophecy to Dolohov. He carries Hermione's unconscious body, insists on staying with Harry rather than raising the alarm alone, and even when his speech is barely comprehensible from the injury, his determination is absolute. 'We'll dake her wid us. I'll carry her.' His broken wand is identified as his dad's old wand, adding personal grief to physical pain.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's DoM battle is significantly compressed. The specific sequence - Dolohov breaking Neville's wand and nose, Neville insisting on staying and carrying Hermione, the 'dad's old wand' detail, the barely-comprehensible speech ('don'd gib id do dem!') - is not rendered in the film corpus. The film shows Neville participating in the battle and 'Well done, Neville!' is called out by Luna, but the specific beats of his physical suffering and dogged refusal to quit are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's DoM battle is Neville's finest hour in OotP: physically broken but morally unbroken, refusing to abandon Harry, carrying Hermione despite everything. The film compresses the battle into spectacle, losing the specific texture of Neville's suffering and resolve. The 'dad's old wand' detail connects his personal loss directly to the fight, making the scene resonate with the St Mungo's setup. Without both, the adaptation loses the payoff of Neville's entire arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Bellatrix uses Cruciatus on Neville / 'I DOE YOU HAB!'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Bellatrix recognises Neville and says 'I have had the pleasure of meeting your parents', Neville roars 'I DOE YOU HAB!' and fights so violently that the Death Eater holding him shouts for someone to Stun him. Bellatrix then tortures him with Cruciatus, and even while screaming in agony and then sobbing at her feet, Neville shouts 'DON'D GIB ID DO DEM, HARRY!' This is the climax of Neville's arc: facing the torturer of his parents, being subjected to the same curse, and still prioritising Harry's mission over his own pain.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does include Bellatrix confronting Neville ('How's Mom and Dad?') and Neville responding 'Better, now they're about to be avenged.' Neville attempts a spell which Bellatrix deflects. However, the Cruciatus torture of Neville does not appear in the film - it is Sirius who is shown being tortured by Voldemort (in Harry's vision). The film's Neville is captured but not tortured, and does not have the agonised-yet-defiant 'DON'D GIB ID DO DEM' moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal_clarification: The film gives Neville a strong line ('Better, now they're about to be avenged') but removes the Cruciatus scene that is the visceral payoff of his parents-connection arc.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Cruciatus scene in the book is the structural climax of Neville's OotP arc: the son of parents tortured by this curse is subjected to it himself by their torturer, and still fights for Harry. Removing it means the film's Neville gets a good line but never pays the personal price that makes his courage genuinely moving. The arc that began with his parents' suffering (itself lost without St Mungo's) and was meant to culminate in this moment is doubly truncated. This is the most structurally significant active scene loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Order of the Phoenix - Prophecy revelation: Neville as alternate Chosen One
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: At the end of OotP, Dumbledore reveals to Harry that the prophecy could have applied to Neville as well - born at the end of July, parents in the Order, parents who escaped Voldemort three times. Voldemort chose Harry, not Neville. This retroactively reframes Neville's entire existence and his parents' fate as being bound to the same prophecy-logic that governs Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes the prophecy text ('the one with the power to vanquish the Dark Lord approaches... neither can live while the other survives') but does not include Dumbledore's explanation to Harry about Neville as the alternate candidate. This information is entirely absent from the film's post-battle conversation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While this revelation is primarily about Harry's arc, it also fundamentally recontextualises Neville - his parents' torture, his upbringing, his entire life was shaped by a choice Voldemort made between him and Harry. The film audience never learns that Neville was the road not taken. This reduces Neville from a figure of structural thematic importance (the mirror-Harry, the one who could have been) to simply a brave friend, losing a dimension of his meaning within the saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 - Slughorn's dinner party on the train: Neville stares at cutlery and asks 'Which one do I use for the soup?'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 50: At Slughorn's train compartment lunch, Neville sits through an uncomfortable ten minutes being interviewed about his tortured, heroic parents. He also actively defends Harry by saying 'We never heard a prophecy' (Book Scene 53), turning geranium pink but still speaking up. He is presented as someone Slughorn is 'reserving judgment on' for potential flair. His presence is grounded in his Ministry heroism and his parentage.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film relocates Slughorn's gathering to a dinner party at Hogwarts and replaces Neville's substantive characterization with a single comedic beat: he stares helplessly at cutlery and asks which fork to use for soup, playing him as socially inept and clueless rather than quietly courageous.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to show Neville has earned his place through bravery and to hint at his heroic lineage. The film reduces him to a buffoon punchline, stripping the moment of any dignity or characterization value and replacing courage/potential with social incompetence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 - Slughorn's Christmas party: Neville appears as a waiter serving drinks, not as an invited guest
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 12-14 and 24: Neville is explicitly recognized publicly as someone who fought Death Eaters at the Ministry. His grandmother is proud he is 'starting to live up to his dad.' Book Scene 50 establishes that Slughorn is reserving judgment on whether Neville has his parents' flair — treating him as a candidate worth evaluating. Neville has social standing earned through his bravery.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neville tells Harry 'I didn't make the cut for the Slug Club. It's okay. He's got Belby handing out towels in the loo,' and is shown serving drinks on a tray — framed as a low-status figure doing menial labor at the party rather than a guest.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This actively contradicts the book's trajectory where Neville, post-Ministry, is gaining recognition and respect. The film instead signals his social irrelevance and low standing. The self-deprecating 'it's okay' delivery also flattens his character into resigned comedy rather than quiet dignity. It damages the book's arc of Neville beginning to be recognized for his own courage and worth.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 - Quidditch tryouts montage: Neville sidesteps Bludgers as a passive bystander joke (repeated twice)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not place Neville at Quidditch tryouts as a spectator joke. More broadly, Book Scenes 14, 24-25, 75-77 establish Neville post-Ministry as someone growing in confidence and receiving genuine recognition — from his grandmother, from McGonagall, and implicitly from his peers. He is shown as earnest and improving, not as a comic prop.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neville appears twice in the Quidditch tryouts montage solely as a sight gag: everyone else flees incoming Bludgers while Neville remains, sidling left then right, used purely for a repeated physical comedy beat with no dialogue or agency.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While minor in isolation, this reinforces a pattern across the film corpus of using Neville exclusively as comic relief — a passive, oblivious figure rather than an increasingly capable and courageous one. It contributes to a cumulative flattening of his post-Ministry growth arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 / Film Scene 4 combined: Absence of Neville's defensive speech protecting Harry from Slughorn ('We never heard a prophecy')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 53: When Slughorn presses Harry about the prophecy, Neville turns 'geranium pink' but speaks up directly: 'We never heard a prophecy.' This is a small but meaningful act of loyalty and quiet courage — Neville choosing to protect Harry even while embarrassed, in front of an intimidating adult.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Slughorn gatherings (train dinner relocated to Hogwarts dinner party, Christmas party) contain no equivalent moment. Neville has no lines of substance in either gathering that demonstrate loyalty, courage, or protectiveness toward Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The omission removes a beat that defines the Harry-Neville friendship dynamic: Neville acting as a loyal ally even under social pressure. Combined with the cutlery joke replacing the train dinner, the film loses all evidence of Neville's active loyalty and replaces it with passive comedy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4: Absence of McGonagall scene validating Neville and pushing back against his grandmother's expectations
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 74-77: McGonagall tells Neville his grandmother should 'be proud of the grandson she's got, rather than the one she thinks she ought to have — particularly after what happened at the Ministry.' Neville turns pink with 'delighted incredulity' at receiving a compliment. McGonagall also reveals Augusta failed her own Charms O.W.L. This scene validates Neville's identity independent of his parents' legacy and is a key step in his arc toward self-acceptance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no equivalent scene. The only Neville material in the corpus is the cutlery joke, the waiter cameo, and the Quidditch montage sidesteps.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the most important Neville scenes in Book 6 — it directly addresses his core wound (living in the shadow of his parents and his grandmother's impossible expectations) and marks genuine emotional progress. Its absence means the film never acknowledges Neville's internal struggle or his growth. This is arc-level damage to his trajectory toward becoming his own person.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 21 (courtyard, Neville steps forward toward Voldemort with Sorting Hat)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Neville is singled out by Voldemort after being identified as the boy who gave the Carrows trouble. Voldemort recruits him, Neville flatly refuses ('I'll join you when hell freezes over'), shouts 'Dumbledore's Army!' to rally the crowd, and is then forcibly placed under the Body-Bind Curse with a burning Sorting Hat as punishment. His defiance is unambiguous and immediate — he never appears to be surrendering.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film stages Neville walking forward voluntarily toward Voldemort with his chin on his chest and his gaze to the ground, so that onlookers (Seamus included) and the audience read it as surrender or collaboration. He is treated with derision ('the best Hogwarts has to offer?'). The framing creates deliberate ambiguity about his intent that does not exist in the book, and removes the spontaneous, defiant rallying cry ('Dumbledore's Army!') that motivates the crowd.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Neville is immediately, loudly defiant — his refusal is the spark that emboldens the survivors. The film undercuts this by visually coding his approach as possible capitulation, delaying the reveal of his intent and stripping the crowd-rallying 'Dumbledore's Army!' shout entirely. His courage reads as a twist rather than a character expression, and the moment loses its function as collective inspiration.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 22 (courtyard, Neville's speech to the crowd)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book gives Neville no extended speech. His defiance is a single blunt line ('I'll join you when hell freezes over') followed by a rallying cry. The moment is brief, sharp, and visceral — consistent with his established voice throughout DH: understated, matter-of-fact courage.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Neville a scripted inspirational monologue ('People die every day... they didn't die in vain... Harry's heart did beat for us') culminating in spitting at Voldemort. The voice is oratorical and sentimental, quite unlike his terse, dry characterisation elsewhere in both corpora.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The speech imposes a generic hero-rallying register onto a character whose entire book appeal is that his bravery is expressed without rhetoric. The book corpus consistently shows Neville speaking matter-of-factly about horrific things ('Doesn't matter. They don't want to spill too much pure blood'). The film speech is out of voice and softens the starkness that makes his courage distinctive.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 23 (entrance hall, Neville steps between Harry and Voldemort and is blasted away)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Neville kills Nagini in a single decisive moment immediately after breaking free of the Body-Bind, drawing the sword from the Sorting Hat in one fluid motion during the chaos of the centaurs' charge. The act is his alone, executed with agency and precise timing. He is not incapacitated before killing the snake.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film splits the sword-drawing and the snake-killing into two separate scenes. In the first (Scene 23), Neville draws the sword but is immediately blasted fifty feet across the hall by Voldemort's spell before he can use it, and the narrative frames this as potentially fatal ('no one could have survived that'). The snake-kill is then completed later (Scene 25) almost incidentally, after Neville recovers off-screen.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's snake-kill is a single climactic flourish of agency: Neville breaks free, draws the sword, and kills Nagini in one unbroken movement. The film fractures this into a failed heroic attempt followed by a later clean-up action, removing the dramatic unity. The interposition of Neville being blasted nearly to death also introduces a survival-spectacle beat that overshadows the killing itself, and the snake-kill in Scene 25 arrives almost as an afterthought while Harry and Voldemort are the main focus.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 15 (marble staircase, Neville tells Harry he is 'mad for Luna')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes no romantic interest between Neville and Luna. Luna's ceiling portrait (book Scene 15-16) shows she treasures Neville as a friend, linked by the word 'friends' repeated in gold. The book corpus contains no hint of Neville having feelings for Luna.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Neville announces mid-battle, 'I'm mad for her! Think it's about time I told her, seeing as there's a pretty good chance we'll both be dead by dawn!' This is played for light comic relief.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film invents a romantic sub-plot for Neville with no book basis. While brief, it is confirmed by the film's epilogue staging (Scene 26: Luna sits down close beside Neville and smiles). This reframes a friendship-based relationship and attaches a romantic-comedy beat to a character whose arc is about courage and resilience, not romance. It also implicitly reduces Luna's independent characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 26 (Great Hall epilogue, Luna sits beside Neville)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book epilogue (Scene 181) shows Neville surrounded by 'a knot of fervent admirers' with the sword of Gryffindor beside his plate — he is celebrated for his heroism in his own right. Luna is not mentioned in his immediate company.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Luna sits close beside Neville and smiles at him in a manner that confirms the romantic framing established in Scene 15, replacing the book's image of Neville as an independently celebrated hero with a romantic-resolution tableau.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book closes Neville's arc with him as a figure of admiration in his own right. The film closes it with a romantic beat that subordinates his heroic resolution to a relationship pay-off the books never establish, slightly deflecting attention from his individual arc completion.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 17 (entrance hall, Neville and Oliver Wood carry Nigel's body)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 133-135 shows Neville carrying Colin Creevey's body in from the grounds. The moment is explicitly weighted: Colin was underage, he sneaked back, and 'he was tiny in death.' Neville hands the body to Oliver Wood and then returns to the darkness to recover more bodies — he 'looked like an old man.' This is a defining beat of Neville's wartime gravity and quiet service.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces Colin Creevey with 'Nigel,' a minor invented film character, stripping the scene of its emotional and thematic weight. The specific pathos of an underage boy who sneaked back to fight — resonant with Neville's own arc of unrecognised sacrifice — is lost.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The substitution of Nigel for Colin removes the specific poignancy the book attaches to this beat. Colin is a character the audience has known since year two; his death and Neville's quiet service in recovering him is a moment of real weight. Replacing him with a generic film-original character drains the scene of its resonance and diminishes Neville's role as a witness and caretaker of the war's cost.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scenes 4-7 (passage and Room of Requirement — absence of Neville's full resistance narrative)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book passage (Scenes 37-83) gives Neville an extended account of the year: the DA's graffiti campaigns, losing Luna at Christmas and Ginny after Easter, Michael Corner being tortured, the Carrows failing to break him, his grandmother being targeted, Dawlish being hospitalised by Gran, Gran's letter saying he is his parents' son, and his consequent decision to disappear into the Room of Requirement. This narrative establishes him as the primary resistance leader at Hogwarts during Harry's absence, with a fully realised arc of escalating stakes and personal cost.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses this to a brief exchange in the passage (Scene 5) covering only the Carrows' punishments and the gash on Neville's face. The year-long resistance campaign, the loss of Luna and Ginny as co-leaders, the DA's communications network, his grandmother's defiance, and the personal cost to Neville are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The missing material is not incidental colour — it is the substance of Neville's arc across Deathly Hallows. Without it, the film's Neville arrives battered but without context for why or at what cost, and the audience cannot appreciate the scale of what he has led and endured. His climactic moments (the speech, the sword) therefore lack the earned foundation the book provides. This is the single largest source of structural damage to the characterisation.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scene 7 (Room of Requirement — Neville's challenge to Harry about trust and fighting together)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 91-113 show Neville pressing Harry directly and with genuine moral weight: 'We're his army... We were all in it together... I don't see why you can't trust us. Everyone in this room's proven they're loyal.' He speaks with earned authority as the year's resistance leader, and his frustration is principled, not merely emotional. He also takes the initiative of calling Luna and Ginny back via the fake Galleons.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses this exchange. Neville asks 'What's the plan, Harry?' and accepts Harry's vague answer without the sustained, principled challenge of the book. The moral tension — Neville's legitimate claim that the DA has fought and bled and deserves to know why they are being excluded — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book exchange is one of the few moments where Neville speaks to Harry as a moral equal and actually challenges him. It reflects his growth into a leader who has earned the right to demand accountability. Removing it reduces Neville to a supportive secondary character and weakens the peer dynamic between him and Harry at the story's climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: DH Part 2 - Film Scenes 18-20 (courtyard before Voldemort's ultimatum — absence of Harry's private conversation with Neville about Nagini)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 137-156 show Harry seeking Neville out deliberately, pulling off the Invisibility Cloak to ensure Neville sees him, lying to protect him ('Course not... this is something else'), and entrusting him with the Horcrux secret as a backup: 'Dumbledore had died knowing that three people still knew about the Horcruxes; now Neville would take Harry's place.' Neville grips Harry's wrist and says 'We're all going to keep fighting, Harry. You know that?' — and pats him on the shoulder before returning to recover bodies. This is Harry consciously choosing Neville as his heir to the secret.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is absent from the film entirely. The Nagini instruction reaches Neville only incidentally — he overhears Harry shouting 'The snake! We've got to kill the snake!' in Scene 23. There is no private moment, no deliberate trust, no Harry choosing Neville.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is the moment Harry formally passes responsibility to Neville, cementing their relationship as something beyond acquaintance. It gives Neville's snake-kill an intentional, entrusted quality — he kills Nagini because Harry asked him to, privately, as the person Harry most trusts with this. The film's accidental overhearing replaces deliberate trust with proximity, fundamentally changing the meaning of the act and the depth of the Harry-Neville relationship.
